messages.text: Take {gift_item}. Better to carry thanks before you need steel.
Here, {gift_item}. I trust you to use it with a cooler head than most.
Then the advice kept its edge. {tested_villager} liked {gift_item}.
That blade was poorly balanced. For {gift_subject}, try {alternative_gift}.
{gift_item} missed clean? Bring {alternative_gift}; better weight for the hand.
That advice had a dull edge. Try {alternative_gift}; it should bite better.
You swung with what I handed you. Next time, choose {alternative_gift}.

openings.text: Mind the grindstone. What do you need?

closings.text: Back to keeping blades honest, then.

lines.text: Rust on a sword is just neglect learning to speak.
Trouble always finds villages. Best be ready.
The golem did good work last night. Still, I keep the blades sharp.
Mind the grindstone. It has no patience for wandering fingers.
A blade tells the truth about its owner sooner or later.
Ready is not the same as eager. A village should know the difference.
I once polished rust off a sword and found three old mistakes underneath.
Weapon jokes are sharp. I keep the dull ones for people who lean too close.
That was dull enough to be safe, at least.
Keeping an edge honest is mostly knowing when to stop grinding.
An unready guard is just confidence standing in the wrong place.
Some nights, the grindstone sounds like preparation instead of work.
Stand back. I know the sound trouble makes when it wants to be casual.
I remember fighting something inside me and losing. You gave me another weapon: morning.
The cure struck true. I remember you standing on the right side of it.
Your face rings like steel, but the battle around it is smoke.
I remember wanting to bite, then wanting to breathe. You were there between them.
I remember you, and I remember being dangerous. Do not make me relive either too quickly.
The blades and watch posts took the thunder badly, but everyone near my station is breathing.
I checked the blades and watch posts first, then the people. Both needed steady hands.
That storm rattled the blades and watch posts; it rattled us more.
Lightning makes every trade feel small. We are safe enough for now.
I will trust the sky again when it stops threatening the roof.
I checked the blades and watch posts for sparks. Then I checked faces for fear.
Smoke gets into everything: lungs, clothes, and the way people talk afterward.
The blades and watch posts can be replaced. People cannot. That is the count that matters.
We saved what hands could reach before the flames decided otherwise.
Fire teaches quick priorities. Water, exits, children, neighbors.
During a raid, the blades and watch posts matters less than who makes it behind a door.
The horns stopped, but my hands still expect more trouble.
We counted survivors before supplies. That is the right order.
Raiders came looking for weakness. They found a village that remembers how to stand.
I saw fear move through the village and courage move faster.
Night trouble always finds the loose latch first. We are fixing those now.
I kept near the blades and watch posts and listened for anyone calling for help.
Dawn did not erase the attack, but it gave us light to count by.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by staying alive.
We are safe enough, though every shadow is getting inspected twice.
The blades and watch posts collected half the desert, but the people made it indoors.
I checked the blades and watch posts, then checked who was coughing from the dust.
Sand in the hinges, sand in the eyes, but no one missing so far.
Harsh wind teaches you which doors really close.
We are safe enough, though the village sounds like it is grinding its teeth.
The blades and watch posts can wait. Warm hands and clear paths matter first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near me found shelter.
Cold works quietly. We are checking on anyone who went quiet too long.
The blades and watch posts froze stiff, but the village kept moving.
We are alright for now. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
